statement: The Governor of Tamil Nadu is appointed by the President under Article 155 and holds office during the President's pleasure for a nominal five-year term under Article 156, continuing until a successor takes over.

Under Article 154 the executive power of the state is vested in the Governor, but under Article 163 a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor except where the Constitution requires the Governor to act in discretion.

Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar has discharged the Tamil Nadu Governor's functions since 12 March 2026, after R. N. Ravi was moved to West Bengal, and was appointed the full-time Governor on 12 October 2026.
Article 161 lets the Governor grant pardons, reprieves and remissions or suspend or commute sentences for offences against state laws, acting on the advice of the state cabinet.
The Governor can promulgate an ordinance under Article 213 when the Assembly is not in session, and it lapses six weeks after the Assembly reassembles unless replaced by an Act.

In S.R. Bommai v Union of India (11 March 1994) the Supreme Court held that whether a ministry has a majority must be tested on the floor of the Assembly, not in the Governor's or President's assessment.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: S.R. Bommai vs Union of India

statement: In Nabam Rebia v Deputy Speaker (13 July 2016) a Constitution Bench held that the Governor cannot summon or advance an Assembly session on his own, outside the advice of the Chief Minister and cabinet, while the government commands a majority.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Nabam Rebia vs Deputy Speaker

statement: In Shivraj Singh Chouhan v Speaker, Madhya Pradesh (13 April 2020) the Supreme Court held that a Governor may direct a floor test for a sitting government when there is objective material suggesting it has lost its majority.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Shivraj Singh Chouhan vs Speaker Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly

statement: Article 164(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment (2003), caps the council of ministers including the Chief Minister at 15% of the Assembly's strength (minimum 12), so Tamil Nadu's 234-member House allows at most 35 ministers.
Under Article 164(4) a minister who is not an MLA must win a seat within six consecutive months or cease to be a minister.
keywords: not a member of the legislature

statement: Article 164(2) makes the council of ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly, so a government falls if it loses a confidence vote.
Article 167 obliges the Chief Minister to communicate cabinet decisions and proposed legislation to the Governor and to furnish information the Governor calls for.
Under Article 166 all executive action is expressed in the Governor's name and the Governor makes the rules of business that allocate work among ministers.
keywords: in the name of the governor

statement: The Advocate General, the state's chief law officer, is appointed by the Governor under Article 165, must be qualified to be a High Court judge and holds office during the Governor's pleasure.

Under Prakash Singh v Union of India (22 September 2006) a state must pick its DGP from the three senior-most officers empanelled by the UPSC, and the DGP gets a minimum two-year tenure regardless of superannuation.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Prakash Singh & Ors vs Union Of India

statement: The Chief Secretary is the senior-most cadre post in the state administration, held by an IAS officer chosen by the state government, and acts as ex-officio secretary to the cabinet.

IAS and IPS officers serving Tamil Nadu belong to All India Services created under Article 312, recruited by the Union but working for the state, which is why their central deputation and discipline involve both governments.

Article 324 vests superintendence of Assembly elections in the Election Commission, and officials on election work are deemed to be on deputation to it (RP Act 1950, s.13CC), which is how it transfers police and civil officers during the model code.

sources.outlet: Vajiram & Ravi explainer on EC transfers

statement: The model code of conduct is a set of Election Commission guidelines, not a statute, that binds parties, candidates and the government from the announcement of the poll schedule until results.
C. Joseph Vijay of the TVK was sworn in as Chief Minister on 10 May 2026 after convincing Governor Arlekar of majority support, becoming Tamil Nadu's 16th Chief Minister.
Vijay's government won its floor test on 13 May 2026 with 144 votes in favour and 22 against, while the DMK walked out.
Congress left the DMK-led alliance to join the TVK government in May 2026, while four other alliance parties backed the TVK-led coalition without formally leaving the alliance.

Tamil Nadu (Madras State until 1969) has had chief ministers since 1952 ranging from C. Rajagopalachari to C. Joseph Vijay, who took office on 10 May 2026 after M. K. Stalin's term (7 May 2021 to 9 May 2026).

The Governor is ex-officio Chancellor of state universities, and in 2022-23 the Assembly passed bills shifting vice-chancellor appointments from the Governor to the state government, which became law after the Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling deemed them assented.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: The State Of Tamil Nadu vs The Governor Of Tamilnadu

statement: Udhayanidhi Stalin of the DMK has been Leader of the Opposition since 11 May 2026; a party needs at least 10% of the Assembly's seats to have its leader recognised in that post.
The Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly is a unicameral house of 234 members elected from single-member constituencies by first-past-the-post for five years, so a majority is 118.
Under Article 189(3) the quorum of the Assembly is ten members or one-tenth of the House, whichever is greater, which is 24 members in Tamil Nadu's 234-seat House.
keywords: house adjourned for want of quorum

statement: The Assembly elects its Speaker and Deputy Speaker from among its members under Article 178, and the Speaker can be removed only by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice under Article 179.
J. C. D. Prabhakar is the Speaker of the 17th Tamil Nadu Assembly elected in 2026.
Article 174 requires the Governor to summon the Assembly so that no more than six months pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.

Article 176 requires the Governor to address the Assembly at the first session after each general election and at the start of each year's first session, setting out the government's agenda in a speech prepared by the government.

Governor R. N. Ravi departed from the government-prepared address in January 2023, prompting a House resolution to record only the printed text, and walked out without reading it in 2024, 2025 and January 2026, citing the national anthem not being played at the start.

Rule 110 of the Tamil Nadu Assembly Rules lets a minister make a statement on a matter of public importance with the Speaker's consent, and no debate is allowed on it when it is made, which is why scheme announcements under it draw opposition protests.

In September 2026 the DMK objected to Chief Minister Vijay using Rule 110 to announce the withdrawal of cases against farmers and teachers, and Speaker J. C. D. Prabhakar ruled the statement did not violate the rule.
During the 18 February 2017 trust vote DMK MLAs, including M. K. Stalin, were evicted from the House by marshals on the Speaker's orders, and Edappadi K. Palaniswami won the vote 122-11.

Article 212 bars courts from questioning the validity of Assembly proceedings on the ground of irregular procedure, which limits challenges to expunctions, suspensions and Speaker's rulings, though the Supreme Court reviews Tenth Schedule decisions.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu

statement: Under Article 199 the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill, and the Governor cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration under Article 200.

The state budget is the annual financial statement laid before the Assembly under Article 202, and when it cannot be passed in time, such as in an election year, the Assembly can pass a vote on account under Article 206 to fund spending for part of the year.

V. N. Janaki's government won a contested confidence vote in January 1988 amid disorder in the House, after which the Rajiv Gandhi government dismissed it and imposed President's Rule on 30 January 1988.

Section 151A of the Representation of the People Act requires a by-election within six months of a vacancy unless the remaining term is under one year or the Election Commission certifies it is difficult to hold one.

sources.outlet: Representation of the People Act, 1951 (bare text, CourtBook)

statement: Under Article 190(3) an MLA's seat falls vacant when the Speaker accepts a written resignation, and the Speaker must reject it if satisfied it is not voluntary or genuine.
Six AIADMK MLAs resigned their seats after the TVK government took office in 2026, the sixth being Karur MLA M. R. Vijayabhaskar on 29 June 2026, with most joining the TVK.
The TVK won both Assembly by-elections held on 6 October 2026, Dharapuram and Madurantakam, which the AIADMK had won in May; outlets differ on the party's resulting strength.
Under the Tenth Schedule an MLA is disqualified for voluntarily giving up party membership or defying the party whip in a vote without condonation, and the Speaker decides the petition.
Since the 91st Amendment (2003) removed the one-third 'split' exception, a defection is protected only as a merger, which requires at least two-thirds of the legislature party to agree.

In Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu (18 February 1992) the Supreme Court upheld the anti-defection law but held that the Speaker's disqualification decisions, acting as a tribunal, are open to judicial review.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu And Others

statement: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v Speaker, Manipur (21 January 2020) the Supreme Court said Speakers should decide disqualification petitions within three months absent exceptional circumstances.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker Manipur Legislative Assembly

statement: Speaker P. Dhanapal disqualified 18 AIADMK MLAs backing T. T. V. Dhinakaran on 18 September 2017, and the Madras High Court upheld this on 25 October 2018 after a split Division Bench verdict.
Tamil Nadu's Legislative Council was abolished with effect from 1 November 1986 after an Assembly resolution moved by the M. G. Ramachandran government on 14 May 1986.

DMK governments tried to revive the Council in 1989, 1996 and 2010, when Parliament passed the Tamil Nadu Legislative Council Act, 2010, but each time the next AIADMK government passed a resolution to drop it, most recently in 2011.

Under Article 200 the Governor may assent to a bill, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or reserve it for the President, and if the Assembly passes a returned bill again the Governor shall not withhold assent.

Under Article 201 the President may assent to or withhold assent from a bill reserved by the Governor, or direct that a non-money bill be returned to the Assembly, which must reconsider it within six months.
On 13 November 2023 Governor R. N. Ravi withheld assent to 10 bills and reserved two for the President, and the Assembly re-passed the 10 bills at a special session on 18 November 2023.

In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025) the Supreme Court held the Governor's reservation of the 10 re-passed bills illegal and, using Article 142, treated them as having received assent.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: The State Of Tamil Nadu vs The Governor Of Tamilnadu

statement: The April 2025 judgment set timelines for Governors: one month to withhold or reserve on cabinet advice, three months when acting against that advice, and one month to assent to a re-passed bill, with delays open to judicial review.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: The State Of Tamil Nadu vs The Governor Of Tamilnadu

statement: Answering a Presidential reference on 20 November 2025, a Constitution Bench said courts cannot set timelines for Governors or the President on bills and that 'deemed assent' is alien to the Constitution, but a court may issue a limited mandamus against prolonged, unexplained inaction.

The November 2025 opinion said a Governor under Article 200 has three options, to assent, to reserve for the President, or to withhold and return the bill with comments, and cannot simply withhold assent and sit on it.

Article 246 divides law-making into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule, and Parliament's law prevails over a state law on a Concurrent subject under Article 254 unless the state law gets Presidential assent.
Public order (entry 1) and police (entry 2) are State List subjects, so law and order is the state government's responsibility.
Intoxicating liquor (entry 8) and agriculture (entry 14) are on the State List, which is why prohibition and liquor retail are decided by the state.
Education, including medical education and universities, is entry 25 of the Concurrent List (it was originally entry 11 of the State List), and electricity is entry 38 of the Concurrent List.

Under Article 356 the President can take over a state's government on a report of constitutional breakdown, a proclamation needs Parliament's approval within two months, lasts six months at a time and cannot normally exceed one year.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: S.R. Bommai vs Union of India

statement: Tamil Nadu has been under President's Rule four times: 31 January 1976 to 30 June 1977, 17 February to 9 June 1980, 30 January 1988 to 27 January 1989, and 30 January 1991 to 24 June 1991.
The Karunanidhi government was dismissed on 31 January 1976 during the Emergency, and the Sarkaria Commission of inquiry was set up to probe corruption charges against it.

The Chandra Shekhar government at the Centre dismissed Karunanidhi's DMK government on 30 January 1991 and imposed President's Rule, months before Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated at Sriperumbudur on 21 May 1991.
Tamil Nadu's share of the states' pool of central taxes was about 4.02% under the 14th Finance Commission, 4.08% under the 15th and 4.097% under the 16th (2026-31), down from 5.39% under the 11th.

sources.outlet: Report of the Sixteenth Finance Commission, Vol. I (indiabudget.gov.in)

statement: The 16th Finance Commission kept the states' share of the divisible pool of central taxes at 41% for 2026-27 to 2030-31.

sources.outlet: Report of the Sixteenth Finance Commission, Vol. I (indiabudget.gov.in)

statement: Under Article 280 the President constitutes a Finance Commission every five years to recommend how central tax proceeds are shared between the Union and the states and among the states.
Under Article 293(3) a state that still owes money to the Centre needs the Centre's consent to borrow, which gives the Union control over state borrowing limits.
Under the fiscal responsibility framework states are generally held to a fiscal deficit of 3% of GSDP, and Tamil Nadu has its own Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2003.

GST compensation transfers to states ended on 30 June 2022, and Tamil Nadu told the 16th Finance Commission it faced an estimated shortfall of nearly Rs 20,000 crore in 2024-25 and had lost control over much of its tax base.

sources.outlet: Report of the Sixteenth Finance Commission, Vol. I (indiabudget.gov.in)

statement: The Centre withheld about Rs 2,152 crore of Samagra Shiksha funds for 2024-25 after Tamil Nadu declined to sign the PM SHRI memorandum, and the state sued in the Supreme Court in May 2025; the court declined urgent hearing in June 2025.

The 84th Amendment (2001) froze the allocation of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats among states on the 1971 census until the first census taken after 2026, so Tamil Nadu's 39 Lok Sabha seats could change after that census.

Chief Minister Stalin hosted a Joint Action Committee on delimitation in Chennai on 22 March 2025, attended by leaders from Kerala, Telangana, Punjab, Karnataka and others, which sought a further 25-year freeze on population-based delimitation.
Article 262 lets Parliament set up tribunals for inter-state river disputes and bar other courts from them, the route used for the Cauvery dispute.

The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's final award of 5 February 2007 allocated 419 tmcft a year to Tamil Nadu, 270 to Karnataka, 30 to Kerala and 7 to Puducherry, and was notified only on 20 February 2013.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: State of Karnataka vs State of Tamil Nadu (Cauvery)

statement: On 16 February 2018 the Supreme Court cut Tamil Nadu's Cauvery share to 404.25 tmcft, raised Karnataka's to 284.75 tmcft, and required Karnataka to deliver 177.25 tmcft a year at Biligundlu.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: State of Karnataka vs State of Tamil Nadu (Cauvery)

statement: The Cauvery Water Management Authority was set up by the Union government on 1 June 2018 under the Supreme Court's 2018 verdict, followed by the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee.

On 13 November 2025 the Supreme Court found Tamil Nadu's application against Karnataka's Mekedatu reservoir report premature, since the Central Water Commission would decide only after the detailed project report and the views of the Cauvery authority and committee.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: State of Karnataka vs State of Tamil Nadu (Mekedatu application)

statement: On 7 May 2014 the Supreme Court struck down Kerala's 2006 law capping the Mullaperiyar dam and allowed Tamil Nadu to store water up to 142 ft, a level reached on 21 November 2014 for the first time in 35 years.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: State Of Tamil Nadu vs State Of Kerala & Anr

statement: The Mullaperiyar dam operates under a 999-year lease signed on 29 October 1886 between the Maharaja of Travancore and the British Secretary of State; the dam sits in Kerala but is operated by Tamil Nadu.

India recognised Sri Lanka's sovereignty over Katchatheevu under the 1974 maritime boundary agreement, and a 1976 agreement barred each country's fishermen from fishing in the other's exclusive economic zone.
In June 2011 the Jayalalithaa government petitioned the Supreme Court that the 1974 and 1976 agreements ceding Katchatheevu were unconstitutional.
Article 345 lets a state legislature adopt one or more languages for official purposes, and Tamil is Tamil Nadu's official language under that power.
Tamil Nadu has followed a two-language policy of Tamil and English since the Assembly adopted Chief Minister Annadurai's resolution of 23 January 1968 scrapping the three-language formula.

The President withheld assent to Tamil Nadu's 2021 bill exempting the state from NEET, which Chief Minister Stalin told the Assembly on 4 April 2025, and the state challenged that decision in the Supreme Court in November 2025.
Tamil Nadu has opposed a national medical entrance test since the Medical Council of India announced NEET in 2012, arguing the syllabus differed from state boards.

The Karunanidhi government set up the P. V. Rajamannar Committee on Centre-state relations, which reported on 27 May 1971 recommending transfer of subjects to the states; sources differ on whether it was constituted in 1969 or 1970.

The Stalin government set up a high-level committee on Union-state relations under former Supreme Court judge Kurian Joseph in April 2025, and Stalin tabled Part I of its report in the Assembly on 18 February 2026.
Tamil Nadu withdrew its general consent for CBI investigations on 14 June 2023, hours after the ED arrested minister V. Senthil Balaji, so the CBI needs case-by-case state permission.
The Enforcement Directorate, a central agency, investigates money laundering under the PMLA and does not need state consent, which is how it acts in Tamil Nadu despite the CBI consent withdrawal.

Tamil Nadu reserves 69% of seats in state educational institutions and state government jobs: 30% for Backward Classes (including 3.5% for BC Muslims), 20% for Most Backward Classes and Denotified Communities, 18% for Scheduled Castes (including 3% for Arunthathiyars) and 1% for Scheduled Tribes.
To shield 69% from the 50% ceiling, Tamil Nadu enacted its 1993 reservation Act, which received Presidential assent and was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 76th Amendment of 31 August 1994.
In Indra Sawhney v Union of India (16 November 1992) the Supreme Court capped reservations at 50% save in extraordinary situations, the ceiling Tamil Nadu's 69% exceeds.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Indra Sawhney vs Union Of India

statement: In I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu (11 January 2007) a nine-judge bench held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure, leaving the 69% law open to review.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: I.R. Coelho vs State Of Tamil Nadu

statement: On 31 March 2022 the Supreme Court upheld the Madras High Court's ruling striking down the 2021 law giving Vanniyars 10.5% within the MBC quota, for lack of quantifiable data.
unit: per cent internal quota struck down

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Pattali Makkal Katchi vs A. Mayilerumperumal

statement: Tamil Nadu's 2009 Act reserves 3% for Arunthathiyars within the 18% SC quota, and the Supreme Court's seven-judge ruling in State of Punjab v Davinder Singh (1 August 2024) upheld sub-classification of Scheduled Castes.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: The State Of Punjab vs Davinder Singh

statement: An all-party meeting chaired by Stalin on 12 November 2022, boycotted by the AIADMK and BJP, rejected the 103rd Amendment's 10% EWS quota and Tamil Nadu has not adopted it for state posts.

The HR&CE (Amendment) Act, 1970 abolished hereditary succession for temple archakas, and in Seshammal v State of Tamil Nadu (14 March 1972) the Supreme Court upheld it while saying appointments must follow Agama rules.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Seshammal & Ors vs State Of Tamil Nadu

statement: The DMK government's order of 23 May 2006 allowing persons of all castes to be appointed archakas was considered by the Supreme Court in Adi Saiva Sivachariyargal Nala Sangam (2015), which required appointments to conform to the Agamas.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: All India Adi Saiva Sivacharyargal Seva vs State of Tamil Nadu (Madras HC)

statement: On 14 August 2021 Chief Minister Stalin handed appointment orders to 58 archakas, including 24 trained at state-run schools under the all-castes scheme, and the Madras High Court upheld the 2020 archaka appointment rules in August 2022.
unit: trained archakas of all castes appointed

statement: Hindu temples in Tamil Nadu are administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department under the HR&CE Act, 1959.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: Seshammal & Ors vs State Of Tamil Nadu

statement: The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) is the state government's agency for investigating corruption by public servants in Tamil Nadu.
Tamil Nadu's Lokayukta was created under the Tamil Nadu Lokayukta Act, 2018, passed in July 2018 and in force from 13 November 2018.

Since the 2018 amendment to the Prevention of Corruption Act, section 17A requires prior approval of the competent authority before police investigate a public servant over official decisions, except in trap cases.

Tamil Nadu's 1982 preventive detention law, popularly the Goondas Act (Gundar Sattam), allows habitual offenders to be detained for up to 12 months, with an advisory board of judges reviewing each detention.

In Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (13 May 2016) the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation under IPC sections 499 and 500, a provision Tamil Nadu governments have often used against critics and the press.

The June 2020 custodial deaths of a father and son in Sathankulam police station were investigated by the CBI, and a Madurai sessions court convicted nine police personnel in March 2026 and sentenced them to death on 6 April 2026.
Child sexual offences in Tamil Nadu are tried under the central POCSO Act, 2012, which sets up special courts and mandatory reporting.
Elections to panchayats and municipalities are run by the Tamil Nadu State Election Commission, not the Election Commission of India, under Articles 243K and 243ZA.
The Assembly unanimously passed a law in February 2016 raising reservation for women in Tamil Nadu's local bodies from the constitutional minimum of one-third to 50%.
In the February 2022 urban local body polls the DMK and allies won over two-thirds of more than 12,800 ward posts and all 21 municipal corporations.
TASMAC, set up in 1983, became the sole retail vendor of liquor in Tamil Nadu after an October 2003 amendment to the Tamil Nadu Prohibition Act, 1937, and private outlets were gone by 2004.

Rajaji's Congress ministry introduced prohibition partially in 1937; it stayed total until the Karunanidhi government suspended it in 1971, was reimposed in 1974, and was lifted again by the MGR government in 1981.

The school midday meal began under Chief Minister K. Kamaraj, launched in Ettayapuram on 17 July 1956 by the education department, and was expanded by M. G. Ramachandran into the Nutritious Noon Meal Scheme from 1 July 1982.
The Chief Minister's Breakfast Scheme for government primary school pupils was launched in September 2022 and covers all 30,122 government primary schools for classes 1 to 5.

Tamil Nadu runs a universal public distribution system rather than the targeted one under the 2013 National Food Security Act, giving all rice card holders free rice of 12-20 kg a month depending on family size.
The Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission, a body under Article 315, recruits for state government posts through the Group exams.
The State Planning Commission, formed in 1971, was renamed the State Development Policy Council by the AIADMK government in 2020 and renamed back in August 2021 by the DMK government.
Aavin is the brand of the Tamil Nadu Co-operative Milk Producers' Federation, the state's dairy cooperative, whose milk prices and procurement rates are set by the government.

TANGEDCO was restructured in 2024 into the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation (TNPDCL), the Tamil Nadu Power Generation Corporation for thermal plants and the Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation for renewables, with the renaming approved on 27 June 2024.
The Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation) was founded on 20 November 1916 in Madras by C. Natesa Mudaliar, T. M. Nair and P. Theagaraya Chetty to press non-Brahmin claims.

The Justice Party won 63 of 98 seats in the November 1920 Madras Presidency elections, which the Congress boycotted, and A. Subbarayalu Reddiar became the first Chief Minister (Premier) under dyarchy.
The Self-Respect Movement against caste hierarchy began in 1925 and was led by E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar).

The first anti-Hindi agitation opposed the Rajaji ministry's compulsory Hindi in Madras Presidency schools from 1937; two protesters died, 1,198 people were arrested, and compulsory Hindi was withdrawn in 1940.

The 1965 anti-Hindi agitation, against Hindi becoming the sole official language from 26 January 1965, left about 70 people dead by official estimates and drew Prime Minister Shastri's assurance that English would continue.
Periyar's movement took the name Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944, after the Justice Party merged under his leadership in 1938.
C. N. Annadurai founded the DMK on 17 September 1949 as a breakaway from Periyar's Dravidar Kazhagam.
Under the 1956 linguistic reorganisation, Madras State lost its Malayalam areas to Kerala and gained five Tamil-majority taluks from Travancore-Cochin.
Madras State was renamed Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969 under Annadurai's DMK government.
C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) of the Congress was Chief Minister of Madras State from 10 April 1952 to 13 April 1954.
K. Kamaraj of the Congress was Chief Minister from 13 April 1954 to 2 October 1963, when he resigned under the Kamaraj Plan to work for the party.
M. Bhaktavatsalam was the last Congress Chief Minister, serving from 2 October 1963 to 6 March 1967, a period that included the 1965 anti-Hindi agitation.
Annadurai became the first DMK Chief Minister on 6 March 1967 and died in office on 3 February 1969.
M. Karunanidhi was Chief Minister five times: 1969-71, 1971-76, 1989-91, 1996-2001 and 2006-11.
M. G. Ramachandran founded the ADMK (later AIADMK) on 17 October 1972 after being expelled from the DMK following a feud with Karunanidhi.
M. G. Ramachandran was Chief Minister from 30 June 1977 until his death on 24 December 1987, apart from a break under President's Rule in 1980.
After MGR's death the AIADMK split between his wife V. N. Janaki, who was Chief Minister from 7 to 30 January 1988, and J. Jayalalithaa, who led the reunited party from 1989.
J. Jayalalithaa was Chief Minister six times between 1991 and 2016, beginning on 24 June 1991 and ending with her death in office on 5 December 2016.
Former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by an LTTE suicide bomber at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on 21 May 1991, during the election campaign.

The Supreme Court voided Jayalalithaa's 2001 appointment as Chief Minister in September 2001 because she stood convicted in the TANSI land case, and O. Panneerselvam was CM from 21 September 2001 until she returned on 2 March 2002 after the Madras High Court acquitted her.

On 27 September 2014 a Bengaluru special court convicted Jayalalithaa in the disproportionate assets case, sentenced her to four years and fined her Rs 100 crore, making her the first sitting Chief Minister forced out by a conviction.
The Karnataka High Court acquitted Jayalalithaa on 11 May 2015, and she returned as Chief Minister on 23 May 2015.
On 14 February 2017 the Supreme Court restored the trial court's conviction of Sasikala and two others in the assets case; proceedings against Jayalalithaa had abated on her death.

sources.outlet: Supreme Court/High Court judgment via Indian Kanoon: State Of Karnataka vs Selvi J. Jayalalitha & Ors

statement: AIADMK ministers joined Vajpayee's government in 1998, resigned on 8 April 1999, and Jayalalithaa withdrew support on 14 April 1999, leading to the government's fall.
The DMK joined the BJP-led NDA for the 1999 Lok Sabha election and Vajpayee's government, then allied with the Congress in 2004, when its alliance swept the state and it joined the UPA government.
Karunanidhi's 2006-11 government distributed free colour TVs to ration-card families, and Jayalalithaa's government from 2011 gave mixers, grinders, fans and free laptops to students.

A special court in Delhi acquitted all accused in the 2G spectrum case, including DMK leaders A. Raja and Kanimozhi, on 21 December 2017; the ED and CBI appealed in March 2018, and on 22 March 2024 the Delhi High Court allowed the CBI's appeal to proceed.
In the 1952 Madras State election the Congress won 152 of 375 seats with 34.88% of the vote, short of a majority, and C. Rajagopalachari became Chief Minister; turnout was 54.75%.
In 1957 the Congress won 151 of 205 seats and K. Kamaraj continued as Chief Minister; turnout was 46.56%.
In 1962 the Congress won 139 of 206 seats with 46.14% and Kamaraj continued as Chief Minister, while the DMK became the main opposition with 50 seats and 27.10%.

In 1967 the DMK won 137 of 234 seats and ended Congress rule, with Annadurai as Chief Minister, even though the Congress, with 51 seats, polled a slightly higher vote share (41.10% to the DMK's 40.69%).
In 1971 the DMK under Karunanidhi won 184 of 234 seats with 48.58% of the vote, its best tally; turnout was 72.10%.
In 1977 the AIADMK won 130 of 234 seats with 30.36% in its first Assembly election and M. G. Ramachandran became Chief Minister.
In 1980, months after his government was dismissed, MGR's AIADMK won 129 of 234 seats with 38.75% and he returned as Chief Minister; turnout was 65.42%.
In 1984 the AIADMK won 132 of 234 seats with 37.03% and MGR won a third term; turnout was 73.47%.
In 1989, with the AIADMK split, the DMK won 150 of 234 seats with 33.18% and Karunanidhi returned as Chief Minister after 13 years; turnout was 69.69%.
In 1991, held weeks after Rajiv Gandhi's assassination, the AIADMK won 164 of 234 seats with 44.39% and Jayalalithaa became Chief Minister, while the DMK won only 2; turnout was 63.84%.
In 1996 the DMK won 173 of 234 seats with 42.07% in alliance with the Tamil Maanila Congress (39 seats) and Karunanidhi became Chief Minister; turnout was 66.95%.
In 2001 the AIADMK won 132 of 234 seats with 31.44% to the DMK's 31 seats and 30.92%, and Jayalalithaa returned as Chief Minister; turnout was 59.07%.

In 2006 the DMK won 96 of 234 seats with 26.46% and Karunanidhi formed a minority government backed by allies such as the Congress (34 seats), while the AIADMK won 61 seats with 32.64%; turnout was 70.82%.
In 2011 the AIADMK won 150 of 234 seats with 38.40% and Jayalalithaa returned as Chief Minister, while Vijayakanth's DMDK (29 seats) beat the DMK (23) to second place.
In 2016 the AIADMK won 136 of 234 seats with 41.06% and the AIADMK became the first ruling party re-elected since 1984, while the DMK won 89 with 31.86%.
In 2021 the DMK won 133 of 234 seats (its alliance 159) with 37.70% and M. K. Stalin became Chief Minister, while the AIADMK won 66; turnout was 73.63%.

In the 23 April 2026 election, counted on 4 May, the TVK won 108 of 234 seats with 34.92% of the vote, short of the 118 majority, against the DMK's 59 (24.19%) and the AIADMK's 47 (21.21%), producing Tamil Nadu's first hung Assembly.
In 2026 the DMK-led alliance won 73 seats in all (DMK 59, Congress 5) and the AIADMK-led NDA 53 (AIADMK 47, BJP 1), and the AIADMK lost its main-opposition status to the DMK.
Turnout in the 2026 Assembly election was a record 85.1% (revised from 84.69%), after a Special Intensive Revision of rolls left about 57.3 million eligible voters.
Outgoing Chief Minister M. K. Stalin lost Kolathur in 2026 and resigned on 5 May, 15 of his ministers were defeated, and Vijay won both Perambur and Tiruchirappalli East, later giving up one seat.
The TVK's 2026 win ended 59 years of DMK or AIADMK rule that began in 1967, making it the first non-Dravidian major party to lead the Assembly since the 1960s.
In the 2019 Lok Sabha election the DMK-led alliance won 38 of Tamil Nadu's 39 seats and the AIADMK, then in the NDA, won only Theni; turnout was 72.44%.
In the 2024 Lok Sabha election the DMK-led INDIA bloc alliance swept all 39 Tamil Nadu seats, while the BJP-led NDA and the separate AIADMK front won none.
After the May 2026 Assembly result the Congress, VCK and IUML MPs moved with the TVK-led coalition, leaving the DMK camp with 27 of Tamil Nadu's Lok Sabha seats and the TVK-led alliance with 12.
unit: Lok Sabha seats with DMK camp

statement: Chief Minister J. Jayalalithaa died in office on 5 December 2016, having been admitted to Apollo Hospital, Chennai, on 22 September 2016, and O. Panneerselvam was sworn in as Chief Minister the next day.

After the Supreme Court convicted V. K. Sasikala on 14 February 2017, ending her bid to become Chief Minister, her nominee Edappadi K. Palaniswami was sworn in on 16 February 2017, replacing O. Panneerselvam, who had rebelled against her.
The Panneerselvam and Palaniswami factions merged in August 2017 and expelled Sasikala from the party in September 2017; she was released from prison in January 2021.
Edappadi K. Palaniswami became AIADMK general secretary on 11 July 2022, the year O. Panneerselvam and two other MLAs backing him were expelled from the party.

The AIADMK left the BJP-led NDA on 25 September 2023, the two fought the 2024 Lok Sabha poll separately and won nothing, and they reunited on 11 April 2025 with Palaniswami as the chief ministerial face.
M. Karunanidhi died on 7 August 2018, and M. K. Stalin, whom he had named his successor in 2013 and who had been working president since January 2017, became DMK president on 28 August 2018.
Police firing on anti-Sterlite protesters in Thoothukudi on 22-23 May 2018 killed 13 people, and the state ordered the copper smelter sealed on 28 May 2018.
The Justice Aruna Jagadeesan Commission reported in August 2022 that police used excessive force at Thoothukudi and recommended action against senior officers.
Mass protests at Chennai's Marina beach in January 2017 against the Supreme Court's ban on jallikattu led the state to pass a law allowing the bull-taming sport.

Actor Sivaji Ganesan left the Congress to found the Thamizhaga Munnetra Munnani on 10 February 1988; allied with the Janaki faction, it lost every seat in 1989, including his own at Thiruvaiyaru, and was dissolved that December.
Actor Vijayakanth founded the DMDK in Madurai on 14 September 2005; contesting all 234 seats alone in 2006, it won only his own seat, Virudhachalam, but polled 8.38%.
Allied with the AIADMK in 2011, the DMDK won 29 seats and Vijayakanth was Leader of the Opposition from 2011 to 2016; he died on 28 December 2023.
Kamal Haasan founded Makkal Needhi Maiam in Madurai on 21 February 2018; he lost Coimbatore South narrowly in 2021, joined the DMK camp, and took a Rajya Sabha seat on 25 July 2025.
Rajinikanth announced his entry into politics on 31 December 2017 but said on 29 December 2020 that he would not launch a party, citing his health.
Actor C. Joseph Vijay founded the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on 2 February 2024, headquartered at Panaiyur, Chennai, saying it would contest the 2026 election.
The TVK held its first state conference at Vikravandi in Villupuram district on 27 October 2024, where Vijay set out the party's ideology.
On 27 September 2025 at least 41 people were killed in a crowd crush at a TVK campaign rally addressed by Vijay near Karur.

On 13 October 2025 the Supreme Court transferred the Karur crush investigation to the CBI under a supervisory committee headed by retired judge Ajay Rastogi; the CBI probe is pending and no court has found any person or party responsible.
The Election Commission recognised the TVK as a state party in Tamil Nadu on 10 September 2026 and confirmed the whistle as its reserved symbol.
M. K. Stalin was sworn in as Chief Minister on 7 May 2021, heading the DMK's first government with a majority of its own since 1996, and served until 9 May 2026.
E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar), who led the Self-Respect Movement and the Dravidar Kazhagam, is the ideological founder of Dravidian politics claimed by the DMK, AIADMK and others.
The Dravidian movement grew from the Justice Party and Self-Respect Movement, and parties descended from it, the DMK and AIADMK, governed Tamil Nadu without a break from 1967 to 2026.

Tamil Nadu has had several actor-politicians as Chief Minister: M. G. Ramachandran, V. N. Janaki, J. Jayalalithaa and, from 2026, C. Joseph Vijay, whose TVK was the first actor-led party since MGR's AIADMK in 1977 to top the poll in its debut Assembly election.

statement: Before 1947 most of present Tamil Nadu formed part of the British Madras Presidency, whose legislature saw Justice Party ministries from 1920 to 1937 and Rajaji's first Congress ministry in 1937.
